facts.text: Subsequent events are kept outside the period figures. On 2026-01-21 the 2034 senior notes of USD 500.0 million were issued and the 2028 senior notes redeemed, and the revolver commitment rose to USD 375.0 million with its maturity moved to 2031-01-21. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a sound view is the direction of earnings. Nine-month EBITDA fell 7.78% while revenue rose 1.05%, so margin compression, not weaker sales, is the problem: the gross profit percentage fell from 33.6% to 32.4% as material, labor and fuel costs rose and the lower-margin Distribution and Manufacturing category grew 33.2%. If that continues, 12-month EBITDA falls further below USD 465.9 million and net leverage rises above 1.37x even with no new debt. If that continues, 12-month EBITDA falls further below USD 465.9 million and net leverage rises above 1.37x even with no new debt. Stabilisation of the gross profit percentage near the FY2025 level of 34.0%, with the add-on proceeds held as cash, would strengthen the view.

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The opposite reading is that the rise in gross leverage is partly a choice. The company issued USD 500.0 million of notes against USD 300.0 million redeemed, and cash is USD 94.0 million higher than at FY2025, which offsets over half of the USD 166.8 million of added debt while the revolver is undrawn; net leverage of 1.37x is low. That reading fails if the cash is spent: dividends, repurchases and acquisitions already exceeded free cash flow by USD 49.1 million in nine months, and a repurchase authorisation of up to USD 500.0 million runs to 2027-03-01. The observable tests are cash and net debt at 2026-12-31, FY2026 EBITDA against USD 493.7 million, and whether the add-on proceeds appear as cash. - Medium: The effect on net debt and net leverage of the USD 250.0 million term loan add-on of 2026-10-27 is not established, because the quarterly report states neither the fees nor how the proceeds will be used. This restricts any pro forma net leverage, and gross principal after the add-on is the only figure that can be stated. The next quarterly report or the current report on the amendment would close it. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 33–34; calculation C74; calculation C75 - Medium: Covenant levels are not established. No executed credit agreement or indenture is supplied, the availability level below which the 1.0x fixed charge test applies is not printed, the net leverage levels that step down the term loan prepayments are not printed, and the revolver borrowing base is not printed. This restricts covenant headroom, effective revolver availability and any statement of capacity; the executed agreements would close it. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 12–13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 47–48; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 125; Source readiness (CP-0) - Medium: The issuer states no EBITDA or adjusted EBITDA, so every ratio uses an EBITDA calculated from operating income and depreciation and amortization, and no adjusted bridge exists. This restricts comparison with agency or covenant definitions and with issuer-defined leverage; earnings releases or a lender presentation would close it. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 96; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 100–103; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3–4 - Low: The guarantors of the 2034 senior notes and of the vehicle and equipment notes are not stated in the notes to the financial statements, and the filings print the lien priorities of the term loan and the revolver together without allocating them. This restricts structural priority and recovery work; the indenture and credit agreements would close it. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 125–126; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 47–48; Source readiness (CP-0) - Low: Various notes payable of USD 1.3 million have no stated security or ranking and are left out of the debt stack, so its cumulative principal is USD 1.3 million below the contractual principal. The effect on cumulative leverage is below the second decimal; the note terms would close it. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 11 - Low: Revolver availability net of letters of credit at 2023-12-31 is not printed in the supplied filings, so the FY2023 undrawn figure in the liquidity table is not supplied; the revolver is stated as undrawn and its commitment as 250.0 at that date. This restricts only the FY2023 liquidity total. Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_ibp-20241231.htm.jsonl, pages 72–74; 10-K_2024-12-31_ibp-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 120 - Low: Source dashes are treated as missing, not zero: asset impairment in FY2023 and FY2025, write-off of debt issuance costs in FY2025 and 9M 2025, the asset impairment add-back in FY2023 and FY2025, proceeds from the term loan in FY2023 and FY2025, debt issuance costs in FY2025 and 9M 2025, swap settlements in 9M 2026 and vehicle and equipment note proceeds in 9M 2026. The subtotals tie without them, so the restriction is on line-by-line reading only; the issuer's confirmation that a dash means nil would close it. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 102–104; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3–5 - Low: Lines that one filing prints and another does not are marked missing. The nine-month cash flow statement prints no asset impairment, deferred income taxes or term loan proceeds line, and the annual cash flow statements print no senior notes lines. This restricts only like-for-like line comparison across filings. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 103–104; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5 - Low: Interest income and gross interest expense are not printed separately because interest expense is shown net, so a gross interest cover cannot be calculated; cover uses cash interest paid, and the split of the 2026 interest paid between the new notes, the redeemed notes and the term loan is not stated. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 102; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5 - Low: The classification of 2026 interest rate swap settlements is not stated: the nine-month cash flow statement prints a dash for swap settlements in investing activities, while interest expense, net carries a benefit of USD 1.9 million. This restricts the alternative cover that nets settlements to the years in which they were reported in investing activities. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 21 - Low: Maintenance and growth capital expenditure are not split, so capital intensity uses total purchases of property and equipment. This restricts any recurring-surplus measure; a disclosure of the split would close it. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 103; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5 - Low: Restricted cash, short-term investments, a single-employer pension obligation, senior secured and subordinated debt totals and a separate non-debt funding float are not printed on the balance sheet, and none is assumed to be zero. Contract liabilities of USD 22.5 million are the only customer-funded item named and are small. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 9; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 137 - Low: The September 2025 balance sheet is not in any supplied filing, so the 9M 2025 balance sheet column is not tabulated and only its closing cash is known from the cash flow statement. This restricts a September 2025 net debt comparison; the third-quarter 2025 report would close it. Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5 - Low: The two stated net proceeds of the 2034 senior notes, USD 490.0 million and USD 492.4 million, are both kept and no figure here depends on either; the issuer's statement of final proceeds is already the later one. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 150; 10-Q_2026-03-31_ibp-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 11; 10-Q_2026-06-30_ibp-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12 - Low: The repayment schedule groups every year after 2030 in one row of USD 966.3 million, which combines the term loan balance due 2031-03-28 and the 2034 senior notes due 2034-02-01, so an annual wall after 2030 is not established. This restricts maturity-year charts beyond 2030. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against an acceptable view is the 2026 pattern: in the nine months to 2026-09-30 dividends, repurchases and acquisitions of USD 245.0 million exceeded free cash flow of USD 195.9 million while operating cash flow fell, gross margin slipped and USD 250.0 million of term loans was added after the quarter end. If the add-on proceeds or further cash fund buybacks, particularly private ones from the chief executive-linked holder, governance would be better described as shareholder-favouring and the risk level would move to high. A persisting buyback pause while EBITDA is below its FY2025 level, add-on proceeds held as cash and disclosure of covenant headroom would support a lower level. The insider's prepaid forward contracts, which cover 4.26% of shares outstanding, settle in November 2026, May 2027 and June 2027 and could change the holder's exposure. facts.text: Overall, Installed Building Products, Inc. presents medium sponsor and governance risk. The key supported behaviour is that dividends, repurchases and cash acquisitions took 97.82% of free cash flow from FY2023 to the nine months to 2026-09-30, and that USD 106.0 million of 2025 repurchases were private purchases from a holder linked to the chief executive, which matters because discretionary cash reaches holders before debt reduction and implies that leverage depends on earnings. Countervailing evidence is audited reporting, extended maturities, no documented liability management and a repurchase pause in the third quarter of 2026. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: Demand is weakening and pricing power is limited, which is the first link in the credit story. In the nine months to 2026-09-30 same-branch installation job volume excluding heavy commercial fell 5.6% while price and mix added only 0.3%, single-family same-branch sales fell 7.7% and single-family starts fell 4.0%, and Fannie Mae forecasts a 3.7% fall in housing starts for 2026. Commercial same-branch sales grew 10.4% and multi-family fell only 1.8%, which limits the decline in installation same-branch sales to 2.9%, but backlog of USD 162.9 million is only 5.48% of FY2025 revenue, so the order book gives little notice of a turn. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a weakening view is the balance sheet: net leverage of 1.37x, liquidity of USD 788.0 million, almost no principal due before 2031 and light capital needs mean a sustained earnings decline would take years to threaten debt service, and commercial same-branch sales growth of 10.4% is cushioning the single-family decline. The opposite risk is that the view is too benign: nine-month free cash flow fell 22.11% while distributions exceeded it, the gross profit percentage fell in both the nine months and the third quarter, and the USD 250.0 million add-on raises floating-rate debt with its use unstated. The view would improve if the gross profit percentage recovered toward 33.6%, if the add-on proceeds were held as cash with repurchases below free cash flow, and if net debt fell in the next filings; it would worsen if LTM EBITDA fell below the USD 419.3 million illustration while distributions continued, if net debt rose without an earnings recovery, or if the revolver were drawn. Pro forma net debt and net leverage after the 2026-10-27 add-on are not established. facts.label: Revenue drivers and pricing power
facts.text: Revenue is cyclical, transactional and driven by volume. In the nine months to 2026-09-30 same-branch installation job volume excluding heavy commercial fell 5.6% and price and mix added 0.3%, so revenue growth of 1.05% came from commercial work and the Other category, partly offset by the residential decline, not from the core single-family job. The mechanism is that single-family volume follows starts, which fell 6.9% in 2025 and 4.0% in the nine months to 2026-09-30, while pricing power is probably limited, since the largest customers are using mortgage rate buydowns to protect affordability, which is analyst inference. The implication is that single-family revenue is unlikely to recover before affordability does and that margin, not revenue, absorbs the shortfall. facts.label: Cost structure and margin resilience
facts.text: Operating leverage works against the company when volume falls. Selling, administrative and amortization expenses were USD 484.7 million in the nine months against USD 470.2 million a year earlier, up 3.08% on revenue growth of 1.05%, so operating income fell 12.14%. Labor is constrained and workers' compensation and medical costs are rising, the oil price rise linked to the Iranian conflict is lifting fuel and freight, and tariffs on imported complementary products could raise material prices. The implication is that margins can be defended against modest volume pressure through price increases, as in 2025, but not against volume loss combined with cost inflation, which is the 2026 position; each further point of gross margin lost is a direct reduction in EBITDA. facts.label: Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds
facts.text: Over the next 12 to 24 months the issuer expects elevated mortgage rates to affect results through the rest of 2026 and Fannie Mae forecasts a 3.7% fall in housing starts for 2026, which pressures revenue, margin and cash-flow visibility. Headwinds are labor, fuel, freight and tariff costs and a continued decline in multi-family units under construction. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The financial transmission runs through free cash flow, which fell 22.11% in the nine months as receivables absorbed more cash, so a downturn would not release working capital as quickly as the issuer's history suggests. Liquidity of USD 788.0 million covers principal due from the rest of 2026 to 2030 8.15x, so the liquidity consequence is a slower build of cash, not a shortfall, unless dividends, repurchases and acquisitions keep running at 125.06% of free cash flow. Management has levers: it bought no shares under the plan in the third quarter of 2026, USD 398.3 million of authorization is optional, acquisitions of USD 63.2 million in the nine months are discretionary, and the dividend is set quarterly. Capex of 2.38% of revenue offers little. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress; the exposure is a leverage that creeps up and a refinancing in 2030 to 2034 that starts from a weaker base. facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, Installed Building Products presents an adequate business profile supported by customer and end-market diversification, a variable cost base and light capital needs, but credit quality is constrained by dependence on single-family housing, margin compression and a financial policy that has returned nearly all free cash flow to holders. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: EBITDA still converts to cash and covers interest 8.76x, though the trend is down. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on net leverage and EBITDA at 2030, when 90.90% of principal comes due and the revolver can spring forward to 2030-12-27, and on how the add-on proceeds are used. The primary downside path is volume loss in single-family housing and margin compression that lifts leverage while distributions continue. Further analysis would need the executed credit agreements, the revolver borrowing base, the use of the add-on proceeds and the guarantor list. Fundamental credit review complete. Top risk: margin compression on falling single-family volume with distributions above free cash flow. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0); calculation C17; calculation C31; calculation C35

### Bottom line

The five filings are enough for a first-pass credit view of Installed Building Products, Inc., with two limits that matter to creditors: the latest balance sheet predates a USD 250.0 million term loan add-on, and no debt agreements or proxy statement were supplied.

Two annual reports and three quarterly reports describe one consolidated registrant and the comparatives checked agree, so period and perimeter are not in doubt. Debt changed materially in 2026, with the 2028 notes replaced by 2034 notes and the revolver enlarged, so year-end and September figures must be kept apart. Governance depth and covenant thresholds cannot be tested beyond what the filings print.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Credit quality is sound: net debt was 1.37x EBITDA on the 12 months to 2026-09-30 and liquidity was USD 788.0 million, though net leverage has risen from 1.14x at FY2025 as shareholder returns and acquisitions outran free cash flow while EBITDA slipped.

### Key findings

The five filings describe one consolidated registrant with a single reportable segment, and the statements tie: assets equal liabilities plus equity at every balance sheet date and each cash flow statement rolls opening cash to closing cash. Because the issuer states no EBITDA, every leverage and cover ratio rests on a calculated EBITDA of USD 493.7 million for FY2025 and USD 465.9 million for the 12 months to 2026-09-30, a house measure that creditors should not read as covenant EBITDA.

Gross leverage eased from 1.86x at FY2023 to 1.80x at FY2025 and then rose to 2.26x on the 12 months to 2026-09-30, while net leverage rose from 1.14x to 1.37x. Debt rose by USD 166.8 million after the January 2026 issue of USD 500.0 million of 2034 notes replaced USD 300.0 million of 2028 notes, and 12-month EBITDA fell by USD 27.8 million, or 5.63%, as the nine-month gross profit percentage slipped to 32.4% from 33.6%. Cash rose by USD 94.0 million, so net debt rose by less, USD 72.8 million; the effect of the October 2026 term loan add-on on net leverage is not established.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a sound view is the direction of earnings. Nine-month EBITDA fell 7.78% while revenue rose 1.05%, so margin compression, not weaker sales, is the problem: the gross profit percentage fell from 33.6% to 32.4% as material, labor and fuel costs rose and the lower-margin Distribution and Manufacturing category grew 33.2%. If that continues, 12-month EBITDA falls further below USD 465.9 million and net leverage rises above 1.37x even with no new debt. Stabilisation of the gross profit percentage near the FY2025 level of 34.0%, with the add-on proceeds held as cash, would strengthen the view.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 35; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 36–38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 41–42; calculation C62; calculation C97; calculation C72; calculation C73; calculation C06; calculation C35

The opposite reading is that the rise in gross leverage is partly a choice. The company issued USD 500.0 million of notes against USD 300.0 million redeemed, and cash is USD 94.0 million higher than at FY2025, which offsets over half of the USD 166.8 million of added debt while the revolver is undrawn; net leverage of 1.37x is low. That reading fails if the cash is spent: dividends, repurchases and acquisitions already exceeded free cash flow by USD 49.1 million in nine months, and a repurchase authorisation of up to USD 500.0 million runs to 2027-03-01. The observable tests are cash and net debt at 2026-12-31, FY2026 EBITDA against USD 493.7 million, and whether the add-on proceeds appear as cash.

| C96 | Capital expenditure intensity, 9M 2026 | 50.0 / 2,246.7 x 100 | 2.23 | % |
| C98 | Variable-rate debt after the 2026-10-27 add-on, before hedges | Term loan principal 487.5 + add-on 250.0 | 737.5 | USD millions |
| C99 | Variable-rate debt not covered by swaps after the add-on | Term loan principal 487.5 + add-on 250.0 - swapped notional 400.0 | 337.5 | USD millions |
## Gaps

- Medium: The effect on net debt and net leverage of the USD 250.0 million term loan add-on of 2026-10-27 is not established, because the quarterly report states neither the fees nor how the proceeds will be used. This restricts any pro forma net leverage, and gross principal after the add-on is the only figure that can be stated. The next quarterly report or the current report on the amendment would close it.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 33–34; calculation C74; calculation C75

- Medium: Covenant levels are not established. No executed credit agreement or indenture is supplied, the availability level below which the 1.0x fixed charge test applies is not printed, the net leverage levels that step down the term loan prepayments are not printed, and the revolver borrowing base is not printed. This restricts covenant headroom, effective revolver availability and any statement of capacity; the executed agreements would close it.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 12–13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 47–48; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 125; Source readiness (CP-0)

- Medium: The issuer states no EBITDA or adjusted EBITDA, so every ratio uses an EBITDA calculated from operating income and depreciation and amortization, and no adjusted bridge exists. This restricts comparison with agency or covenant definitions and with issuer-defined leverage; earnings releases or a lender presentation would close it.

- Low: The guarantors of the 2034 senior notes and of the vehicle and equipment notes are not stated in the notes to the financial statements, and the filings print the lien priorities of the term loan and the revolver together without allocating them. This restricts structural priority and recovery work; the indenture and credit agreements would close it.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 125–126; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 47–48; Source readiness (CP-0)

- Low: Various notes payable of USD 1.3 million have no stated security or ranking and are left out of the debt stack, so its cumulative principal is USD 1.3 million below the contractual principal. The effect on cumulative leverage is below the second decimal; the note terms would close it.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 11

- Low: Revolver availability net of letters of credit at 2023-12-31 is not printed in the supplied filings, so the FY2023 undrawn figure in the liquidity table is not supplied; the revolver is stated as undrawn and its commitment as 250.0 at that date. This restricts only the FY2023 liquidity total.

- Low: Source dashes are treated as missing, not zero: asset impairment in FY2023 and FY2025, write-off of debt issuance costs in FY2025 and 9M 2025, the asset impairment add-back in FY2023 and FY2025, proceeds from the term loan in FY2023 and FY2025, debt issuance costs in FY2025 and 9M 2025, swap settlements in 9M 2026 and vehicle and equipment note proceeds in 9M 2026. The subtotals tie without them, so the restriction is on line-by-line reading only; the issuer's confirmation that a dash means nil would close it.

- Low: Lines that one filing prints and another does not are marked missing. The nine-month cash flow statement prints no asset impairment, deferred income taxes or term loan proceeds line, and the annual cash flow statements print no senior notes lines. This restricts only like-for-like line comparison across filings.

- Low: Interest income and gross interest expense are not printed separately because interest expense is shown net, so a gross interest cover cannot be calculated; cover uses cash interest paid, and the split of the 2026 interest paid between the new notes, the redeemed notes and the term loan is not stated.

- Low: The classification of 2026 interest rate swap settlements is not stated: the nine-month cash flow statement prints a dash for swap settlements in investing activities, while interest expense, net carries a benefit of USD 1.9 million. This restricts the alternative cover that nets settlements to the years in which they were reported in investing activities.

- Low: Maintenance and growth capital expenditure are not split, so capital intensity uses total purchases of property and equipment. This restricts any recurring-surplus measure; a disclosure of the split would close it.

- Low: Restricted cash, short-term investments, a single-employer pension obligation, senior secured and subordinated debt totals and a separate non-debt funding float are not printed on the balance sheet, and none is assumed to be zero. Contract liabilities of USD 22.5 million are the only customer-funded item named and are small.

- Low: The September 2025 balance sheet is not in any supplied filing, so the 9M 2025 balance sheet column is not tabulated and only its closing cash is known from the cash flow statement. This restricts a September 2025 net debt comparison; the third-quarter 2025 report would close it.

- Low: The two stated net proceeds of the 2034 senior notes, USD 490.0 million and USD 492.4 million, are both kept and no figure here depends on either; the issuer's statement of final proceeds is already the later one.

- Low: The repayment schedule groups every year after 2030 in one row of USD 966.3 million, which combines the term loan balance due 2031-03-28 and the 2034 senior notes due 2034-02-01, so an annual wall after 2030 is not established. This restricts maturity-year charts beyond 2030.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 11; calculation C77

- Low: Purchase obligations under two supply agreements are stated in pounds of material, not amounts, and only one fixed-price contract has a stated minimum of USD 10.8 million. This restricts a money measure of purchase commitments.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 28

spans.text: # Business and governance for Installed Building Products, Inc.
## Request

Business and governance review for Installed Building Products, Inc. (issuer ibp-1580905) as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is ownership and control, governance and capital allocation behaviour, the operating model and the issuer's history, taken from the five supplied filings and nothing else.
## Sources
| Source | Document | Document date | sha256 | Use |

| 10-K_2024-12-31_ibp-20241231.htm.jsonl | Annual report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024 | 2025-02-27 | 43fc427d223aed274776a9d6ca5fde2f55d2cbd24780a26db884964bf5d24025 | Related-party repurchase of 2024 and 2023 comparatives |

| 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl | Annual report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025 | 2026-02-26 | 03b8de0e297ca73f1d424064b74b046864a2893576a799a6a3b13af45122b35e | Business, ownership, related parties, acquisitions, capital returns, subsequent events |

| 10-Q_2026-03-31_ibp-20260331.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 31, 2026 | 2026-05-07 | b51cc01569723de4f80fa088d333477b6826156f97750b77d9b78d776c80ed58 | Related-party note and 2026 events |

| 10-Q_2026-06-30_ibp-20260630.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended June 30, 2026 | 2026-08-06 | 0fb52476a0a914dcabac5d2ccf6fcd69e5693e27d34e8893dab18a8ab8d4d520 | 2026 events checked for related-party repurchases |

| 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended September 30, 2026 | 2026-11-05 | d00afa049acfbef203a56f297d83bd5f47f5a6c78105d5dbe18860b16e387f13 | 2026 acquisitions, capital returns, related parties, subsequent events |
| Supplied analysis | Module | sha256 | Use |
| Source readiness | CP-0 | b0c4fcfe23a4a76917b7f6da67197053f764a1c8156a2ccb4fe03a69916503d4 | Source scope, version differences and gaps; no governance conclusion is taken from it |
No external source was used, and the run settings are not listed as a source.
## Findings
### Bottom line

Governance is acceptable for creditors but not conservative: the chief executive, who is also chairman, beneficially owns about 14.5% of the stock, and dividends, buybacks and acquisitions have absorbed almost all free cash flow since FY2023.

Business risk is moderated by breadth: the top ten customers are only 14% of revenue, insulation is 58% of revenue and commercial work is 17%. The business is cyclical, though, and 2026 volumes and margins are falling. The filings document no sponsor, no creditor-adverse transaction and no liability management, but they omit the proxy statement and the executed debt agreements, so board independence and restricted-payment capacity are not established.
### Key findings

Control is influential but not absolute, and the roles are concentrated. Jeffrey W. Edwards is president, chief executive and chairman and beneficially owned about 14.5% of the stock at the end of 2025, enough to influence elections and major transactions without controlling them, and the certificate lets him pursue corporate opportunities himself. For creditors the mechanism is conflict between one holder's interests and lenders', not a sponsor exit, because the filings name no sponsor, no fund life and no monitoring fee. The chief financial officer also sits on the board, and the number of independent directors is not established.

Related-party dealing is small in revenue but carries the main governance flag, private buybacks from a holder linked to the chief executive. In 2025 the company bought shares in three private deals for USD 106.0 million, 61.41% of its FY2025 repurchases by value and 52.94% by share count, each at a 3.0% discount to the prior day's price, and one deal of USD 20.7 million in 2024. The discount favours the company, but the cash goes to an insider and rises with cash capacity. Related-party sales were USD 25.0 million, 0.84% of revenue, and no related-party repurchase appears in the 2026 quarterly reports.

Basis: 10-K_2024-12-31_ibp-20241231.htm.jsonl, page 140; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 142–143; 10-Q_2026-03-31_ibp-20260331.htm.jsonl, page 24; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 26–27; calculation C31; calculation C32; calculation C34; calculation C36

Capital allocation is shareholder-heavy and leaves little room for debt reduction from cash flow. From FY2023 to the nine months to 2026-09-30 free cash flow was USD 1,026.7 million, dividends and repurchases took USD 741.4 million and cash acquisitions USD 262.9 million, together 97.82% of free cash flow. The 2026 position resembles FY2024 more than FY2025: in the nine months to 2026-09-30 dividends, repurchases and acquisitions took 125.06% of free cash flow, against 126.73% in FY2024 and 103.62% in FY2025. Repurchases are the flexible lever, USD 6.3 million in FY2023 against USD 145.3 million in FY2024, and none is shown in the third quarter of 2026, so creditors depend on that restraint continuing.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 103–104; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5; calculation C25; calculation C26; calculation C27; calculation C30; calculation C12; calculation C20; calculation C18; calculation C19

Acquisitions are a repeated, cash-funded programme, small beside free cash flow in most years but not trivial. The company has completed more than two hundred acquisitions since 1999 and aims to acquire at least USD 100.0 million of revenue each year; cash paid was USD 59.6 million, USD 88.6 million and USD 51.5 million in FY2023 to FY2025 and USD 63.2 million in the nine months to 2026-09-30. No acquisition-specific borrowing is documented, but acquired earnings are not stated, and the audit report flags goodwill of the Distribution unit, so integration value is not established.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 6; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 85; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 146–147; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 29; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 99–101; calculation C27; calculation C24

The operating model is diversified by customer and product but tied to one housing cycle. Insulation is 58% of revenue, commercial 17%, the top ten customers 14% and the largest customer about 4%, while installers are paid by completed job and the issuer calls its cost structure highly variable. Single-family, the largest end market, is weakening, with same-branch volume growth of -5.6% in the nine months to 2026-09-30, and the lower-margin Other category grew 33.2%, so gross margin is falling.

Debt-market conduct is creditor-neutral to supportive on the evidence read. The 2028 notes were redeemed in full and replaced with 2034 notes, the revolver was enlarged and extended to 2031, and no waiver, exchange offer, priming or restructuring is described; the added USD 250.0 million of term loans after the quarter end has no stated use, so willingness cannot be separated from capacity, which cannot be tested without the executed agreements.
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against an acceptable view is the 2026 pattern: in the nine months to 2026-09-30 dividends, repurchases and acquisitions of USD 245.0 million exceeded free cash flow of USD 195.9 million while operating cash flow fell, gross margin slipped and USD 250.0 million of term loans was added after the quarter end. If the add-on proceeds or further cash fund buybacks, particularly private ones from the chief executive-linked holder, governance would be better described as shareholder-favouring and the risk level would move to high. A persisting buyback pause while EBITDA is below its FY2025 level, add-on proceeds held as cash and disclosure of covenant headroom would support a lower level. The insider's prepaid forward contracts, which cover 4.26% of shares outstanding, settle in November 2026, May 2027 and June 2027 and could change the holder's exposure.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 33–34; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 62; calculation C12; calculation C04; calculation C37
### Limitations

- The proxy statement for the 2026 annual meeting was not supplied, so board independence, committee structure, director holdings and pay are not established; the finding that governance is acceptable therefore rests on audited reporting and the absence of creditor-adverse transactions, not on tested board checks.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 157

- No executed credit agreement or indenture was supplied, so restricted-payment baskets and their usage are not established; the finding that buybacks and dividends are discretionary cannot be tied to a legal limit, and the risk level could move either way once the baskets are read.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 124

- Free cash flow in the allocation comparison is calculated from operating cash flow and purchases of property and equipment, and acquired earnings are not stated, so the acquisition finding rests on cash spent rather than value received.

- Ownership facts are dated 2025-12-31 and the filings read cover related-party repurchases only through the 2026 quarterly reports, so later share transactions or the outcome of the forward-contract settlements could change the related-party finding.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Fundamental credit quality is sound but weakening: low leverage and wide liquidity absorb the falling margins of a housing-dependent installer, and the main creditor exposure is financial policy, because shareholder returns and acquisitions have taken almost all free cash flow.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C12; calculation C26; calculation C44

Net debt was USD 637.5 million, 1.37x EBITDA for the 12 months to 2026-09-30 against 1.14x at FY2025, and liquidity was USD 788.0 million; pro forma net debt and net leverage after the USD 250.0 million term loan add-on of 2026-10-27 are not established. Nine-month EBITDA fell 7.78% while revenue grew 1.05%, yet only USD 96.7 million of principal falls due before 2031, so the risk is gradual leverage drift, not a liquidity event.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 2–3; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 33–34; calculation C13; calculation C11; calculation C05; calculation C06; calculation C29
### Key findings

Business risk is moderate: the company is one of the largest US insulation installers, spread across many customers and several building products, but it remains tied to a single housing cycle. The top ten customers are 14% of FY2025 net revenue and the largest about 4%, insulation is 58% of revenue and the commercial end market 17%, so no customer or product can by itself break cash flow, while single-family housing, the largest end market, sets the volume trend for most of the business.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 20; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C49; calculation C50; calculation C51; calculation C52

Demand is weakening and pricing power is limited, which is the first link in the credit story. In the nine months to 2026-09-30 same-branch installation job volume excluding heavy commercial fell 5.6% while price and mix added only 0.3%, single-family same-branch sales fell 7.7% and single-family starts fell 4.0%, and Fannie Mae forecasts a 3.7% fall in housing starts for 2026. Commercial same-branch sales grew 10.4% and multi-family fell only 1.8%, which limits the decline in installation same-branch sales to 2.9%, but backlog of USD 162.9 million is only 5.48% of FY2025 revenue, so the order book gives little notice of a turn.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 41; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 20; calculation C63; calculation C64; calculation C66; calculation C61; calculation C59; calculation C68; calculation C67; calculation C65; calculation C56; calculation C83

Margin is the weak point of the credit: the gross profit percentage fell to 32.4% in the nine months from 33.6% a year earlier and to 31.8% in the third quarter from 34.0%, because material, labor and fuel costs rose and the lower-margin Distribution and Manufacturing category grew 33.2%. Selling, administrative and amortization expenses grew 3.08% on revenue growth of 1.05%, so operating income fell 12.14% and nine-month EBITDA fell 7.78%; EBITDA for the 12 months to 2026-09-30 was USD 465.9 million against USD 493.7 million for FY2025, a margin of 15.56% against 16.62%. The variable cost structure protects direct labor and material cost when volume falls, but it does not protect administrative cost, so the cushion is thinner than the cost description suggests.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 37; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 42; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 14; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C70; calculation C71; calculation C72; calculation C73; calculation C69; calculation C80; calculation C06; calculation C82; calculation C05; calculation C01; calculation C02; calculation C07; calculation C08

Cash generation is still strong but is being distributed, so deleveraging from cash flow is not happening. Free cash flow was USD 300.8 million in FY2025, 60.93% of EBITDA, and capital needs are light at 2.38% of revenue, but nine-month free cash flow fell 22.11% to USD 195.9 million. Dividends, repurchases and acquisitions took USD 245.0 million in the nine months, 125.06% of free cash flow, and 97.82% of free cash flow from FY2023 to 2026-09-30, so net debt rose to USD 637.5 million at 2026-09-30 from USD 564.7 million at FY2025; pro forma net debt after the 2026-10-27 add-on is not established.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C20; calculation C21; calculation C25; calculation C22; calculation C24; calculation C40; calculation C43; calculation C44; calculation C13; calculation C14

The balance sheet is the main support and is not under strain: net debt was 1.37x EBITDA at 2026-09-30 against 1.14x at FY2025, total debt was 2.26x against 1.80x, and EBITDA covered cash interest 8.76x against 12.04x. Liquidity was USD 788.0 million, with cash of USD 415.9 million and no revolver draw, and it has not been below USD 766.6 million at any 2026 quarter end. The USD 250.0 million add-on of 2026-10-27 lifts contractual principal to USD 1,313.0 million, 2.82x EBITDA on a principal basis; its effect on net debt and net leverage is not established because the filing gives the use of the proceeds as general corporate purposes and fees without amounts.

Refinancing risk is deferred, not removed. Only USD 96.7 million of principal falls due from the rest of 2026 to 2030, covered 8.15x by liquidity, and 90.90% of principal, USD 966.3 million, falls due after 2030, in the term loan of 2031-03-28 and the 2034 notes. The revolver matures 2031-01-21 but springs 91 days ahead of any material debt maturity, which would bring it to 2030-12-27 if the term loan counts as one, so 2030 is the first year in which refinancing capacity is tested.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 11–13; calculation C29; calculation C87; calculation C31; calculation C30; calculation C35

The interest burden is rising and becomes more rate-sensitive. Cash interest paid was USD 53.2 million over the 12 months to 2026-09-30 against USD 41.0 million in FY2025. Interest swaps fix USD 400.0 million of the term loan until 2028-12-14, leaving USD 87.5 million floating at 2026-09-30, but the add-on is floating: the issuer says each percentage point of rates adds USD 2.5 million to annual interest expense, and unless a new swap is added, which the filings do not mention, USD 337.5 million of term debt is unhedged. The Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate in September 2026 and mortgage rates peaked above 7%, so the tightening that holds back housing also lifts the cost of this debt.

The chief executive, who is also chairman, beneficially owns about 14.5% of the stock, USD 106.0 million of 2025 buybacks, 61.41% of that year's repurchases, were private purchases from a holder linked to him, and USD 398.3 million of repurchase authorization remains, although no shares were bought under the plan in the third quarter of 2026. Whether the add-on proceeds are held as cash or distributed will decide whether net leverage keeps rising.

With LTM EBITDA 10% lower at USD 419.3 million and net debt and cash interest unchanged, net leverage would be 1.52x and EBITDA cover 7.88x, while liquidity of USD 788.0 million would not change; the credit would weaken materially only if lower earnings coincided with distributions above free cash flow and more floating-rate debt. ### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a weakening view is the balance sheet: net leverage of 1.37x, liquidity of USD 788.0 million, almost no principal due before 2031 and light capital needs mean a sustained earnings decline would take years to threaten debt service, and commercial same-branch sales growth of 10.4% is cushioning the single-family decline. The opposite risk is that the view is too benign: nine-month free cash flow fell 22.11% while distributions exceeded it, the gross profit percentage fell in both the nine months and the third quarter, and the USD 250.0 million add-on raises floating-rate debt with its use unstated. The view would improve if the gross profit percentage recovered toward 33.6%, if the add-on proceeds were held as cash with repurchases below free cash flow, and if net debt fell in the next filings; it would worsen if LTM EBITDA fell below the USD 419.3 million illustration while distributions continued, if net debt rose without an earnings recovery, or if the revolver were drawn. Pro forma net debt and net leverage after the 2026-10-27 add-on are not established.

### Limitations

- The executed credit agreements, the indenture and the revolver borrowing base were not supplied, so the conclusion that liquidity is wide rests on stated cash and undrawn commitments and could be lower if borrowing is restricted or a covenant tightens.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 47–48; Source readiness (CP-0)

- The filings stop at the quarterly report signed on 2026-11-05 and give neither the fees nor the use of the add-on proceeds, so the leverage conclusion can move either way: net debt is unchanged by the add-on only if the proceeds are held as cash.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 33–34; Financial foundation (CP-1)

- Revenue by end market is stated only for commercial, so how much of the weakness comes from single-family work cannot be sized, and the sensitivity of EBITDA to housing starts could be larger or smaller than the segment trends imply.

- The downside illustration assumes a 10% fall in a calculated EBITDA that the issuer does not state, so the stressed leverage and cover are indicative of direction and size only and are not forecasts.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C84

- No rating, market price or sponsor view is in the filings, so access to capital markets in a downturn is judged from the maturity profile and the January 2026 notes issue alone, and the refinancing conclusion would change if markets or ratings turned.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 122–126; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 11–12; Financial foundation (CP-1)
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strength 1: low net leverage and a wide liquidity buffer. Net debt was 1.37x EBITDA and liquidity USD 788.0 million at 2026-09-30, against USD 96.7 million of principal due from the rest of 2026 to 2030. The mechanism is time: a decline in earnings has to be deep and long before debt service is threatened, and the revolver is undrawn. The implication is that near-term default risk is low even though the trend is negative, subject to the add-on's effect on net debt, which is not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C12; calculation C26; calculation C29; calculation C87

Strength 2: a long maturity profile after the January 2026 refinancing. Of principal, 90.90% falls due after 2030 and the 2034 notes are fixed-rate, so refinancing and rate risk on most of the debt is deferred. The implication is that refinancing capacity is tested from 2030, when the revolver can spring forward to 2030-12-27, not in the current trading downturn.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 11–13; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 52; calculation C31; calculation C35

Strength 3: light capital needs and a variable cost base support cash conversion. Purchases of property and equipment were 2.38% of FY2025 revenue and free cash flow was 60.93% of EBITDA, while the issuer describes installers as paid by completed job and says it can release cash from inventory and receivables when sales soften. The implication is that earnings convert to cash even in a soft year, though light capex also means little extra cash can be found by cutting it.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 14; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C25; calculation C21; calculation C20

Strength 4: diversification by customer and by end market. The top ten customers are 14% of net revenue, the largest about 4%, commercial work is 17% of revenue and grew 10.4% same-branch in the nine months, and insulation is 58% of revenue with the rest spread over other installed products. The implication is that no single counterparty failure or product shock dominates cash flow, and the commercial and multi-family work partly offsets weak single-family volume.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; calculation C49; calculation C50; calculation C52; calculation C68; calculation C51

Strength 5: scale and installer retention. The company is one of the largest insulation purchasers in the United States and buys most products directly from manufacturers, and installer monthly turnover was 3.2% against 4.0% for the US construction industry. The implication is purchasing leverage and a stable skilled workforce, which help to defend margins, though the 2026 margin trend shows these advantages are not sufficient on their own.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 7; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 20; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 22; calculation C54; calculation C55; calculation C70

Weakness 1: dependence on single-family housing. Single-family is the largest end market, starts fell 6.9% in 2025 and 4.0% in the nine months to 2026-09-30, and single-family same-branch sales fell 7.7%. Installation work follows construction activity and the backlog is only 5.48% of annual revenue. The implication is that earnings are cyclical and visibility is short, so a turn in demand would show in results before the backlog signals it, and a recovery is unlikely before mortgage affordability improves.

The mechanism is that price and mix of 0.3% do not offset volume of -5.6% or cost inflation in materials, labor and fuel. ### Company description

Installed Building Products is one of the largest US installers of insulation for new homes. It also installs waterproofing, fire-stopping, garage doors, gutters, blinds, shower doors, closet shelving and mirrors from a national branch network that serves all 48 continental states and the District of Columbia, and it runs regional distribution businesses and cellulose insulation manufacturing, 5% and 2% of FY2025 net revenue. Installation is the only reportable segment and was 92% of third-quarter 2026 net revenue; the company has completed more than 200 acquisitions since 1999.

The model supports cash-flow visibility only in part. Revenue is earned job by job from builders and follows construction activity, and the backlog of USD 162.9 million at the end of 2025 was only 5.48% of that year's revenue. Installation is a gating phase, since interior work cannot proceed until insulation passes inspection, and most of the ten largest customers have been served for at least two decades, which supports retention but does not protect volume. The implication for creditors is that debt service rests on the balance sheet and on cost flexibility rather than on contracted revenue.

### Ownership and group structure

The company is publicly held and is the borrower and issuer of all its debt, owns its subsidiaries outright, and its restricted subsidiaries guarantee the term loan and the revolver; the guarantors of the 2034 notes are not named in the notes. No sponsor is identified. Jeffrey W. Edwards is president, chief executive and chairman and beneficially owned about 14.5% of the stock at the end of 2025, enough to influence elections and major transactions without controlling them, and the certificate lets him pursue corporate opportunities himself.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 62; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C47

The credit relevance is financial policy rather than structure. Related-party sales are only 0.84% of revenue, but private repurchases of USD 106.0 million in 2025 from a holder linked to the chief executive were 61.41% of the year's repurchases, and Business & governance rates the overall governance risk as medium. The implication is that leverage tolerance is set by a board and a founder-chairman who have so far returned almost all free cash flow to holders, with no covenant level in the supplied documents to bind them.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 142–143; Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C48; calculation C45; calculation C46; calculation C44
### Revenue drivers and pricing power

Revenue is cyclical, transactional and driven by volume. In the nine months to 2026-09-30 same-branch installation job volume excluding heavy commercial fell 5.6% and price and mix added 0.3%, so revenue growth of 1.05% came from commercial work and the Other category, partly offset by the residential decline, not from the core single-family job. The mechanism is that single-family volume follows starts, which fell 6.9% in 2025 and 4.0% in the nine months to 2026-09-30, while pricing power is probably limited, since the largest customers are using mortgage rate buydowns to protect affordability, which is analyst inference. The implication is that single-family revenue is unlikely to recover before affordability does and that margin, not revenue, absorbs the shortfall.

Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 41; calculation C63; calculation C64; calculation C06; calculation C58; calculation C61

The offsets are real but partial. Commercial same-branch sales grew 10.4% and the commercial end market has risen from 11% of revenue in 2013 to 17% in FY2025, multi-family same-branch sales fell only 1.8% in the nine months against a 16.3% fall in national multi-family completions, and the customer base is not concentrated: the top ten customers are 14% of revenue. The company says it realised price increases in 2025 to offset earlier material cost increases but may find it harder to raise prices in the rest of 2026 and beyond if housing demand slows. The implication is that revenue is not structurally declining or concentrated, but is exposed to a cycle that has not yet turned.

### Cost structure and margin resilience

Direct costs are variable but the margin is not being defended in 2026. Materials and labor are the largest expenses, most installation employees are paid by completed job, and the issuer describes a cost structure in which a significant portion of operating expenses is linked to volume. Even so, the gross profit percentage fell to 32.4% in the nine months from 33.6%, and to 31.8% in the third quarter from 34.0%, on higher material prices, labor costs and fuel, a mix shift toward the lower-margin Other category and higher freight from distribution and manufacturing activity.

Operating leverage works against the company when volume falls. Selling, administrative and amortization expenses were USD 484.7 million in the nine months against USD 470.2 million a year earlier, up 3.08% on revenue growth of 1.05%, so operating income fell 12.14%. Labor is constrained and workers' compensation and medical costs are rising, the oil price rise linked to the Iranian conflict is lifting fuel and freight, and tariffs on imported complementary products could raise material prices. The implication is that margins can be defended against modest volume pressure through price increases, as in 2025, but not against volume loss combined with cost inflation, which is the 2026 position; each further point of gross margin lost is a direct reduction in EBITDA.

### Capital intensity and cash conversion

Capital intensity is low and conversion is good. Purchases of property and equipment were 2.38% of FY2025 revenue, free cash flow after cash interest was USD 300.8 million, or 60.93% of EBITDA, and the issuer says it can release inventory and receivables when sales soften. Seasonality matters for liquidity timing: sales and profit are weakest in the first quarter and working capital builds through summer and autumn, and the company has used its revolver for short-term working capital in the past.

The 2026 pattern is weaker. Nine-month free cash flow fell 22.11% to USD 195.9 million and receivables absorbed USD 42.3 million of cash against USD 17.5 million a year earlier, so the working capital release the issuer describes is not automatic. Cash interest rose to USD 53.2 million on a 12-month basis from USD 41.0 million. The implication is that EBITDA still converts to cash well above interest and capital needs, but that surplus has been committed to dividends, repurchases and acquisitions rather than to debt reduction, and capex cuts would release little.

### Porter's five forces in credit terms

Competitive rivalry is moderate and local. The industry is highly fragmented, with one other large national contractor, several regional contractors and numerous local ones, and competition rests on quality and timeliness of service, knowledge of local building codes, pricing, relationships and reputation. Pricing is the channel through which rivalry reaches creditors: price and mix of only 0.3% against volume of -5.6% means the company is not recovering cost inflation in a soft market, which supports the margin compression finding.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 22; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; calculation C64; calculation C63

The threat of new entrants is not established from the filings. They name local code knowledge, relationships and reputation as the basis of competition and list no entry barriers, and the company's history of acquiring local installers suggests the main competitive response to small rivals is purchase, not exclusion. Credit implication: no evidence supports a strong moat, so margins should not be assumed to be structurally protected.

The threat of substitutes is limited within the service but real within the product mix. Fiberglass and cellulose were 83% of insulation installation sales and spray foam 17%, and the choice between them changes ticket size and margin rather than removing the installer. Credit implication: substitution moves revenue per job, not the need for installation, so it is a second-order driver of EBITDA.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 8

Buyer power is moderate. Single-family builders are a fragmented group where the top 100 builders hold about 49% of the market, the largest customer is about 4% of revenue and the top ten about 14%, so no buyer can dictate terms alone, but the largest customers are publicly traded homebuilders using mortgage rate buydowns to protect affordability. This is analyst inference, since the filings do not describe pricing negotiations. Credit implication: builder margin pressure is a plausible channel to installer pricing, which would add to the volume weakness.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 18; 10-K_2025-12-31_ibp-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 20; calculation C49; calculation C50

Supplier power is meaningful. The three largest suppliers are 35% of material purchases, there are few large fiberglass manufacturers that have cut capacity in past cycles and caused industry-wide allocations, and the company says it may have more difficulty raising selling prices to offset supplier increases as demand slows. Credit implication: material cost and availability shocks reach gross margin before they can be priced through, and a capacity cut by manufacturers during the current downturn could cause allocation just when volume recovers.
### PEST factors in credit terms

Economic and political factors are material to this credit and social and technological factors are not primary drivers on the supplied evidence. Mortgage rates peaked above 7% in the third quarter of 2026 after the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds rate in September 2026, which curtails housing demand and raises the cost of the floating-rate term loan; the issuer expects to be affected for the rest of 2026. Inflation raises material, labor and fuel costs and weakens affordability. Tariffs on imported complementary products and uncertainty over trade and fiscal policy could raise material prices. The credit implication is that the same macro tightening hits volume, margin and interest cost together.

### SWOT in credit terms

Strengths that support credit: low net leverage and wide liquidity, a long maturity profile, light capital needs with good cash conversion, and diversification by customer and end market. Weaknesses that constrain credit: dependence on single-family housing, falling margins, distributions that exceed free cash flow, and rising interest cost with untested covenant terms.

Opportunities that could improve credit: a fall in mortgage rates, which the issuer expects would ease pressure on demand, continued commercial and multi-family growth, and use of the add-on proceeds to hold cash or repay debt rather than fund distributions. Threats that could weaken it: further falls in single-family starts, tariff and fuel cost inflation, a supply cut by fiberglass manufacturers, a faster pace of repurchases or acquisitions funded by debt, and a higher rate environment on the floating-rate term debt.

### Financial profile and credit quality

The financial profile rests on four supports: low net leverage of 1.37x, liquidity of USD 788.0 million, a maturity profile with 90.90% of principal due after 2030, and cash conversion of 60.93% of EBITDA in FY2025. Four constraints offset them: gross margin falling to 32.4%, free cash flow distributed in full, interest cover down to 8.76x from 12.04x, and covenant, borrowing-base and guarantor terms that cannot be tested. The trend is negative at the margin, since LTM EBITDA is 5.63% below FY2025 and net leverage is 1.37x against 1.14x at FY2025, and the key missing datapoints are covenant headroom, availability under the borrowing base, the use of the add-on proceeds and any rating. Pro forma net debt and net leverage after the 2026-10-27 add-on are not established.

### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over the next 12 to 24 months the issuer expects elevated mortgage rates to affect results through the rest of 2026 and Fannie Mae forecasts a 3.7% fall in housing starts for 2026, which pressures revenue, margin and cash-flow visibility. Tailwinds are commercial work, growing 10.4% same-branch, multi-family work, where the issuer expects an extended backlog to support 2026 share gains, total backlog that rose to USD 162.9 million from USD 126.3 million at the end of 2025, and the Distribution and Manufacturing businesses, growing 33.2%, which the company says improve procurement but currently dilute margin. Headwinds are labor, fuel, freight and tariff costs and a continued decline in multi-family units under construction. The credit implication, on analyst inference and not a company statement, is that EBITDA is more likely to stay near or below USD 465.9 million than to recover in the short term, with no liquidity or refinancing consequence before 2030 unless distributions continue to exceed free cash flow.

Over three to five years the issuer cites an aging housing stock, many homeowners locked into low mortgage rates and housing shortages as supports for repair and remodel and new construction demand; these are management views that the filings do not quantify. The credit implication is that the cycle should eventually turn, but refinancing of the term loan and the 2034 notes falls in 2030 to 2034, so the recovery needs to be visible in earnings and net leverage before then to keep refinancing terms undemanding.

### Downside scenario

A realistic downside begins with mortgage rates staying above 7% and single-family starts falling again in 2027 after the 4.0% fall in the nine months to 2026-09-30. The first operational break is volume: job volume, already down 5.6%, falls further while price and mix of 0.3% cannot offset material, labor and fuel costs, so the gross profit percentage slips below 32.4% and operating expenses, which grew 3.08% in the nine months of 2026, do not fall with volume. If LTM EBITDA fell 10% to USD 419.3 million, net leverage would be 1.52x and cover 7.88x on the September net debt and interest, before the add-on whose effect on net debt is not established.

Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 36; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 37; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 38; 10-Q_2026-09-30_ibp-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 41; Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C61; calculation C63; calculation C64; calculation C70; calculation C80; calculation C84; calculation C85; calculation C86

The financial transmission runs through free cash flow, which fell 22.11% in the nine months as receivables absorbed more cash, so a downturn would not release working capital as quickly as the issuer's history suggests. Liquidity of USD 788.0 million covers principal due from the rest of 2026 to 2030 8.15x, so the liquidity consequence is a slower build of cash, not a shortfall, unless dividends, repurchases and acquisitions keep running at 125.06% of free cash flow. Management has levers: it bought no shares under the plan in the third quarter of 2026, USD 398.3 million of authorization is optional, acquisitions of USD 63.2 million in the nine months are discretionary, and the dividend is set quarterly. Capex of 2.38% of revenue offers little. Resilience appears sufficient to avoid liquidity distress; the exposure is a leverage that creeps up and a refinancing in 2030 to 2034 that starts from a weaker base.

### Overall credit view

Overall, Installed Building Products presents an adequate business profile supported by customer and end-market diversification, a variable cost base and light capital needs, but credit quality is constrained by dependence on single-family housing, margin compression and a financial policy that has returned nearly all free cash flow to holders. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: EBITDA still converts to cash and covers interest 8.76x, though the trend is down. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on net leverage and EBITDA at 2030, when 90.90% of principal comes due and the revolver can spring forward to 2030-12-27, and on how the add-on proceeds are used. The primary downside path is volume loss in single-family housing and margin compression that lifts leverage while distributions continue. Further analysis would need the executed credit agreements, the revolver borrowing base, the use of the add-on proceeds and the guarantor list. Fundamental credit review complete. Top risk: margin compression on falling single-family volume with distributions above free cash flow.
